objective.statement: Build the scale of F major, lowering a note with a flat.
successCriteria: I know F major needs one flat: B flat.
I know why we write B♭ and not A♯.
I can write the scale of F major in both clefs.

explanation.text: F major starts on F. With only white keys the pattern goes wrong at the 4th note: the step from the 3rd to the 4th is a tone, but the pattern needs a semitone. We fix it by lowering B to B flat.

music.textAlternative: The scale of F major in the treble clef: F G A B flat C D E F.

explanation.caption: F major: F G A B♭ C D E F. One flat, on the 4th note.

music.textAlternative: The scale of F major in the bass clef.

explanation.caption: The same scale in the bass clef.

explanation.text: We write B flat and not A sharp. They are the same key on the piano, but a scale needs each letter name once: F G A B C D E. If we wrote A sharp we would skip B and use A twice.
Sharp keys (G, D) raise the 7th and 3rd notes. F major goes the other way and lowers the 4th note.

music.textAlternative: The scale of F major with B flat as the 4th note, each note linked to its key.

steps: Tap F, G, A, then B flat. The B flat is a black key just left of B.
Compare B natural: from A to B is a tone, but the pattern needs a semitone between degrees 3 and 4.
B flat gives the semitone. Carry on up to the next F.
demonstration.textAlternative: The scale of F major with B flat as the 4th note, each linked to its keyboard key.

recap: F major has one flat: B♭.
We write B♭, never A♯, so each letter is used once.
The pattern is the same in every major key.
